summary:
Moldova's anti-discrimination statute names both sexual orientation and gender identity. Law No. 2 of 2023 lists gender identity, and separately sexual orientation, among grounds protected from "any kind of discrimination"; an employment discrimination ban covering sexual orientation has been in force since 1 January 2013, and Article 11 of the audiovisual media code, effective 1 January 2019, prohibits broadcasting incitement to hatred founded on intolerance, including on grounds of sexual orientation. Hate speech and hate crimes have been criminal offences since 2022 with both grounds named, and the equality law was amended in 2023 to cover them. Consensual sex between men has been legal since 1995 and the age of consent was equalised in 2002. ILGA-Europe ranked Moldova last among 49 European countries for LGBT legislation in 2012 and 23rd by 2023.

Enforcement does not match the statute. The ILGA-Europe Annual Review 2024 records hate speech as a serious problem with no meaningful state response, a finding the European Commission's country report echoes, and notes that political hate speech rose during the election period. Amnesty International's 2025 report describes discrimination against LGBTI people as commonplace and freedom of expression and assembly as arbitrarily restricted, with impunity for past violations. A 2024 ECOM legislative analysis, benchmarked against international standards and built on a survey of local partner organisations, identifies legal barriers for LGBT people and people living with HIV in access to justice and in the operation of hate-crime and discrimination provisions.

Changing legal name and gender marker is permitted but conditional on a psychiatric diagnosis confirming "transgenderism". The mismatch this creates in ordinary transactions is documented: a trans woman was refused bank service because her documents did not match her appearance, and the Equality Council confirmed discrimination and recommended preventive measures.

Public assembly is contested. Pride has been held since 2002 but has repeatedly been banned or cancelled. In May 2008 the mayor banned the parade the evening before, police stood by while crowds surrounded and attacked participants, and the European Court of Human Rights ruled in 2012 that the cancellation violated the convention. The May 2017 march was cancelled by police shortly after it began when Orthodox groups attacked participants, and then-president Igor Dodon publicly endorsed the attacks. In May 2018 police used tear gas to repel counter-protesters and the march completed. Moldova Pride 2024 proceeded openly with participants of all ages.

Partner recognition is absent. The Constitution defines marriage as the union of a man and a woman, and there is no same-sex marriage or civil union, so a trans visitor whose relationship would be read as same-sex under birth-sex status has no access to spousal recognition, residence rights or the next-of-kin protections attached to marriage.

In Russian-occupied Transnistria, legislation adopted in the reporting period prohibits the promotion of "non-traditional sexual relations", per Amnesty International's 2025 report.

Social attitudes remain hostile. The Equality Council study "Prejudices and Marginalization in Moldova 2022", published in January 2023, found acceptance of LGBT+ people extremely low: 79% would not accept LGBT+ neighbours, 60% would not accept them as work colleagues, the social-distance score stood at 5.7, and marginalisation increased during 2022. Politicians frequently make derogatory remarks about the community.

Impunity extends to attacks on advocates: in May 2019 a human rights lawyer representing GENDERDOC-M suffered an arson attack on her car in central Chisinau, and police declined to investigate on the ground that the damage was not "significant".

Official acknowledgement of the problem exists. Following reporting on a transgender detainee, the authorities stated that homophobia persists in state institutions and that they are training staff and preparing stricter penalties for discrimination and harassment.
tangentialFactors:
Parliament passed on 23 May 2013 a bill banning propaganda of prostitution, paedophilia and "any other relations than those related to marriage and family in accordance with the Constitution and the Family Code", carrying fines; it was signed on 5 July 2013 and took effect on 12 July 2013. It did not explicitly prohibit "propaganda" of homosexuality but could be read that way, and the interpretable content was removed by a bill passed on 11 October 2013.

Moldova voted against the UN Human Rights Council's first resolution on sexual orientation and gender identity on 17 June 2011. The resolution, adopted 23 votes to 19, expressed grave concern at violence and discrimination on those grounds, including against transgender people, and established a UN reporting process.
localsOnly:
The clearest documented case of institutional treatment of a trans person is custodial. Igor Brumarețchi, a transgender man from Dubna village in Soroca district, was registered female at birth in 1972 and had his documents changed to male in 2007. Over a four-year detention in Moldova's penitentiary system, mostly at Penitentiary No. 6 in Soroca, he was held alone in unsanitary, rat-infested cells for long periods in the disciplinary isolation unit, presented as being for his own safety, while his request for placement in sector 12, the unit for detainees requiring protection, was refused. He describes forced strip body searches, staff calls over the intercom telling him to "go to the gynaecologist", staff opening his bathroom door, and being called "Natașa" at roll-call. He says only self-harm and hunger strikes got him heard. The National Penitentiary Administration replied that he was held alone "at his own written request", that no rights were violated, and that the discrimination claims were unconfirmed. Brumarețchi says he will sue in Moldovan courts and at the European Court of Human Rights; Ziarul de Gardă notified the Ombudsman and GENDERDOC-M. Reporting in April 2025 corroborated three years of isolation at the same institution.

Sub-national law has repeatedly targeted the community and been struck down. On 30 April 2013 the Parliament of Gagauzia approved a bill forbidding "propaganda" of homosexuality, bisexuality and transness, with no administrative sanctions or fines but with provisions banning registration of LGBT-related organisations and banning LGBT-related clubs and entertainment establishments; a court invalidated it on 20 June 2013 for violating freedom of speech and human rights. Several cities and districts enacted "propaganda" bans with no sanctions: Bălți on 23 February 2012, Drochia on 27 March 2012, Cahul on 29 March 2012 and Ceadîr-Lunga on 10 April 2012. The Bălți Court of Appeals ruled on 28 February 2013 that the northern city's ban was unconstitutional and violated human rights.

The Ministry of Health has stated in an official letter that homosexuality is not considered a disease and that medical services are accessible regardless of sexual orientation.
outOfScopeNotes:
No survey data specific to transgender people's social acceptance is available in the sources; the Equality Council's 2022 figures measure attitudes to LGBT+ people generally, and the material reviewed records no documented statement on societal tolerance of transgender people specifically.

The Brumarețchi case is unresolved. The National Penitentiary Administration denies that his rights were violated and says the discrimination claims were unconfirmed; he has said he will bring proceedings in Moldovan courts and at the European Court of Human Rights, and no outcome is recorded.

Whether the Transnistria legislation is being enforced, and against whom, is not sourced.

The account of Moldova Pride 2024 comes from a travel publication and describes the atmosphere of the event rather than legal conditions.
